lead: Mesh current analysis gives each window of a circuit one invented current and writes KVL round that window. Node voltage analysis gives each node one voltage above a 0 V reference and writes KCL there. Both produce the smallest set of simultaneous equations — one per mesh, or one per non-reference node — instead of one equation per element. Every circuit simulator builds these same matrices internally, and anyone solving a bridge or a two-source network by hand uses them before reaching for superposition or Thevenin's theorem.
prereq: You need: Chapter 1.3 for KVL and KCL, and Chapter 1.4 for reading resistances and branches off a circuit.

sections.h3: Mesh current analysis: one unknown per window

blocks.text: Series-parallel reduction works only when resistors combine. A bridge, a ladder or a network with two sources in different branches does not fold down. You need a method that always works and gives the fewest equations.

A mesh is a window of a flat (planar) circuit: a loop with no other loop inside it. In mesh current analysis you invent one current for each window and draw all of them clockwise. That mesh current is a real branch current only in branches on the outer edge. In a shared branch the real current is the difference of the two mesh currents.

Why invent currents? Once the mesh currents are known every branch current follows, and KCL holds at every node by itself, because each node has mesh currents entering and leaving in pairs. Only KVL is left to enforce, and there are exactly as many independent loops as windows.

items: Redraw the circuit flat and count the windows m. Draw i₁ to i_m all clockwise, in amperes.
Self resistance R₁₁: add every resistor inside mesh 1. It multiplies i₁ with a plus sign.
Shared resistance: the resistor common to meshes 1 and 2 enters as −R_shared, because the two clockwise currents oppose each other there.
Right side: add the voltage sources that drive current clockwise in that mesh. A source pushing anticlockwise enters negative.
Solve the m equations, then convert to the branch currents asked for.

blocks.text: R₁₁ i₁ + R₁₂ i₂ = V₁   and   R₂₁ i₁ + R₂₂ i₂ = V₂
blocks.where: R₁₁ and R₂₂ are the total resistances inside mesh 1 and mesh 2 (Ω); R₁₂ = R₂₁ = minus the resistance shared by the two meshes (Ω); i₁, i₂ are the clockwise mesh currents (A); V₁, V₂ are the sums of the source voltages driving current clockwise in mesh 1 and mesh 2 (V).

blocks.text: A current source on the outer edge belongs to one mesh only, and it fixes that mesh current outright: a 5 A source driving clockwise in mesh 2 means i₂ = 5 A, and one unknown disappears.

A current source shared by two meshes is harder. Its voltage is unknown, so KVL round either mesh cannot be written — you would carry a symbol with no value. Use a supermesh. Remove the branch holding the source, treat the two windows as one big loop, and write a single KVL round the outer path, skipping the source. The unknown source voltage cancels between the two meshes and never appears. That is equation one. Equation two is the constraint the source itself imposes: i₁ − i₂ = I_s, with the sign fixed by the arrow of the source.
Two unknowns, two equations, always solvable.

sections.h3: Node voltage analysis: one unknown per node

blocks.text: Node voltage analysis uses KCL instead of KVL. Choose one node as the reference and call its voltage 0 V — usually the bottom wire, or the node with the most connections. Every other node then has a voltage measured from it. A node voltage is not a branch voltage: the voltage across a resistor is the difference of the two node voltages at its ends.

items: Label the other n − 1 nodes V₁, V₂ … in volts. These are the unknowns.
At each non-reference node write KCL: currents leaving through resistors = currents entering from sources.
A voltage source joined to the reference node fixes that node voltage directly, so no equation is needed for it.
Solve, then take differences to get branch voltages.

blocks.text: Σ (V_node − V_neighbour) / R = Σ I entering
blocks.where: each term is one resistor R (Ω) between the node being written and a neighbour node; V_node and V_neighbour are their voltages above the reference (V); the right side adds the source currents feeding that node (A).

blocks.text: A voltage source sitting between two non-reference nodes has an unknown current, so KCL at either end cannot be written. Draw a closed surface round both nodes — a supernode — write one KCL for the surface, and add the constraint V_a − V_b = V_s. If that source touches the reference node, skip the supernode: the node voltage is simply V_s.

sections.h3: Matrix form and which method to pick

blocks.text: Both methods give linear equations, so write them as a resistance matrix times a current vector equals a source vector. For two unknowns solve by substitution; for three or more use elimination or Cramer's rule, where the determinant is Δ = R₁₁R₂₂ − R₁₂R₂₁ and i₁ = (V₁R₂₂ − V₂R₁₂)/Δ.

Count before you start. A connected flat circuit with b branches and n nodes has m = b − n + 1 meshes and n − 1 independent node equations. Use whichever is smaller. If they tie, avoid work: node analysis suits many parallel branches and many current sources; mesh analysis suits a planar ladder with several voltage sources.

figure.caption: Each row is one mesh equation, read as 6i₁ − 4i₂ = 8 and −4i₁ + 10i₂ = 2. The diagonal entries are each mesh's own resistance, and the two shared 4 Ω terms are equal and negative.

spec.title: Mesh equations in matrix form
spec.aria: A coefficient array with rows for mesh 1 and mesh 2: 6, −4, 8 and −4, 10, 2, where the shared 4 Ω terms are the off-diagonal entries.

examples.question: Two windows of a circuit share a 4 Ω resistor. Mesh 1 also contains an 8 V source and a 2 Ω resistor; mesh 2 also contains a 2 V source and a 6 Ω resistor. Both sources drive current clockwise in their own mesh. Find i₁, i₂ and the current in the shared resistor.
steps: Mesh 1 self resistance = 2 + 4 = 6 Ω. Shared resistor with mesh 2 = 4 Ω, entered as −4i₂. Source sum = +8 V, because the 8 V source drives clockwise. Equation: 6i₁ − 4i₂ = 8.
Mesh 2 self resistance = 4 + 6 = 10 Ω. Shared resistor with mesh 1 = −4i₁. Source sum = +2 V. Equation: −4i₁ + 10i₂ = 2.
Shared 4 Ω resistor carries i₁ − i₂ = 2 − 1 = 1 A, from the mesh 1 side towards the mesh 2 side.
examples.answer: i₁ = 2 A, i₂ = 1 A, and the shared 4 Ω resistor carries 1 A from the mesh 1 side to the mesh 2 side.

traps: Forgetting the minus sign on the shared resistance term. With both mesh currents clockwise, the neighbour's current always opposes your own through the shared resistor, so the term is −R_shared.
Wrong sign on a source. A source whose rise is in the direction of the mesh current is positive; if it drives anticlockwise it enters the right side as negative.
Writing an ordinary mesh equation or node equation across a source that has no resistance in series with it. That branch needs a supermesh or a supernode plus the constraint equation.
Reporting a mesh current as the branch current. In any shared branch the real current is the difference (or sum) of the two mesh currents.

In node analysis, missing a resistor connected to the node, or adding a source current on the wrong side. Current entering a node is positive on the right-hand side; current leaving through a resistor is (V_node − V_neighbour)/R.

quiz.q: What does one mesh current represent, and where is it a real branch current?
quiz.a: A fictitious current circulating clockwise round one window of the circuit. It equals the real branch current only in branches on the outer edge, not shared with another mesh.

quiz.q: Why is the shared resistance term negative in the mesh equations?
quiz.a: Both mesh currents are drawn clockwise. In the shared resistor they flow in opposite directions, so the voltage drop caused by the neighbour's current subtracts from the drop caused by the mesh's own current.

quiz.q: A mesh has self resistance 5 Ω and shares a 2 Ω resistor with mesh 2. A 10 V source drives current clockwise in it. Write its mesh equation.
quiz.a: Self term 5i₁, shared term −2i₂, source +10 V: 5i₁ − 2i₂ = 10.

quiz.q: In a node analysis the reference is 0 V. A node V is joined to a 10 V node through 2 Ω and to the reference through 3 Ω. No sources inject current at V. Find V.
quiz.a: KCL: (V − 10)/2 + V/3 = 0. Multiply by 6: 3V − 30 + 2V = 0, so 5V = 30 and V = 6 V.

quiz.q: A connected flat circuit has 4 nodes and 7 branches. Which method needs fewer equations, and how many?
quiz.a: Meshes = b − n + 1 = 7 − 4 + 1 = 4 equations. Node equations = n − 1 = 3. Node voltage analysis needs 3 equations, so use it.

quiz.q: Why does a current source shared by two meshes force a supermesh instead of two ordinary mesh equations?
quiz.a: The voltage across an ideal current source is set by the rest of the circuit and is unknown, so KVL round either mesh would contain an unknown symbol. Removing the source branch and looping round both meshes cancels that voltage; the source current then supplies the second equation, i₁ − i₂ = I_s.

quiz.q: What is a supernode and what two equations does it give?
quiz.a: Two non-reference nodes joined by a voltage source, treated as one closed surface. One KCL is written for the whole surface, plus the constraint V_a − V_b = V_s.

beyond: Not for the exam. Circuit simulators do not use plain node analysis; they use modified nodal analysis, the same node equations with one extra unknown current per voltage source, so sources never need a supernode. The matrix is large and sparse, and it is factorised once and reused at every time step. Power-grid and chip-level checks solve millions of these nodes. Search for modified nodal analysis, sparse LU factorisation, and spanning-tree loop finding if you want to see how a computer picks the loops.
